title: Tens Jump, Ones Hop
big_idea: Add and take away tens without carrying
child_idea: A jump of ten changes only the tens digit. A hop of one changes only the ones digit. For a bigger step, jump the tens first, then hop the ones.

topics: Mental calculation: a 2-digit number plus or minus tens, without renaming (syllabus 2.7)
A 2-digit number plus or minus ones, without renaming
Number line jumps as a picture of adding and taking away
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. Term 1 goes beyond the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose; it is not MOE-aligned and must not be called that on child or parent pages. In this lesson Start here stays inside P1 mental calculation of a 2-digit number plus or minus tens or ones without renaming (syllabus 2.7), explored first with bundles, bars and number lines. Think harder (a two-digit step split into a jump and a hop) and Go further (two jump sizes, a chain of jumps) go beyond P1 by splitting a 2-digit step into a jump and a hop.

contest_moves: split the second number into tens and ones (jump, then hop)
the order of the steps does not change where you land
fewest jumps with two jump sizes
objectives: Add and take away a multiple of ten from a 2-digit number in your head, knowing that only the tens digit changes (34 + 20 = 54, 54 - 20 = 34).
Add and take away a few ones without passing a ten (34 + 3 = 37, 58 - 3 = 55), knowing that only the ones digit changes.
Split a step such as 34 + 25 into a jump of tens and a hop of ones, and say where you land after each part.
Draw a number line with jumps and hops, and use it to explain an answer.

remember: Count in tens from any number (3, 13, 23 ...)
Read a 2-digit number as tens and ones (46 is 4 tens and 6 ones)
Count on a few ones from a tens number (40 and 5 more is 45)
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20 and showing a number with fingers or a picture. Nothing from an earlier Term 1 lesson is needed except what the warm-up re-teaches with bars and squares. A child who did the holiday course will know counting in tens.
holiday_topics_revisited: Skip counting in 10s (Count with the Frog)
joining_cold.note: Lessons 5 to 7 are among the hardest to miss in Term 1 (plan, section 2). A child who misses Lesson 6 watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2 before Lesson 7, which uses jumps to find a gap.

child: The tens bars and ones squares from the kit page (workbook page 6), cut out by a grown-up before the lesson and kept in an envelope. They are the kit from the first lesson of the term; a child who joined later needs them too.
A coin (for the number path game in the Try at home ideas)
The printed workbook (pages 1 to 5) and the kit page
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
tutor: A slide deck and the kit bars and squares to show on camera if you wish
A visible clock or a timer on your own device (the deck has no timer slide)
kit_pages: Tens bars (9) and ones squares (20), printed on page 6 of the workbook; the same cut-outs as Lesson 1
materials.notes: No ruler is needed in the lesson; a child who has one at home may use it to draw straight number lines. Nothing needs to be bought. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Children need a little clear floor space for the movement break; small things never go near the mouth or ears.

workbook.home_hint: Use your bars and squares, or draw the jumps.
workbook.header: Addition and Subtraction: tens jump, ones hop

kits.title: Kit page: tens bars and ones squares
kits.intro: A grown-up cuts these out before the lesson. A bar is a ten. A square is a one. These are the kit from the first lesson of the term, so keep them in an envelope.

workbook.hint_p1: Use your kit or a drawing. A bundle of 10 is a bar in your kit. Say your answer out loud, then write it.
workbook.hint_p3: Use your kit or draw the jumps and hops. Then write how you know. Choose any question, in any order.

timing.notes: A 2-minute opening (the routine is known from Lesson 1), so Explore has 16 minutes. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.
skip_order: In a slow class the workbook runs about 3 minutes over: take it from the 5-minute flex buffer and shorten choice time, not the exit ticket
optional items and extra quick questions first
then any quick-fire in the mini-lesson

sneak_peek.q1: Mei has the sticks in the picture. Then she gets another bundle of 10 sticks. How many sticks does Mei have now? You may draw.
sneak_peek.q2: Ravi says 43 + 20 = 45. Is Ravi right? Write Yes or No. Then write how you know.
sneak_peek.a2: No. 43 + 20 = 63. 20 is 2 tens, so the tens digit changes, not the ones.

opening.say: If you are watching the recording: hello! Get a pencil, paper, your workbook and your kit of bars and squares. Pause or rewind any time.
opening.action: Gather your workbook, pencil, paper and kit. Press play when ready.

remember.say: Recording: join in! Say the numbers out loud. Pause if you need longer.
remember.action: Play along. Say each number before the video does.

sneak.say: Recording: pause now and try both puzzles on your paper. Guessing is fine. Press play for the next part.
sneak.action: Pause. Try both puzzles on your own paper. A guess is fine.

explore.say: Recording: pause each time I ask. Build the number with your bars and squares, then press play to check.
explore.action: Pause. Build each number with your kit. Write what you notice.

mini.say: Recording: keep watching and copy the jumps and hops onto your paper. Rewind if you miss a step.
mini.action: Watch and copy the jumps and hops. Rewind any step you missed.

break.say: Recording: stand up and join in! Big jumps for tens, small hops for ones.
break.action: Stand up and jump the tens and hop the ones.

work.say: Recording: pause now and do workbook page 1. When you finish a page, press play to check it.
work.action: Pause. Do page 1, then play to check. Then page 2. Then choose a page to try.

talk.say: Recording: pause. Tell a grown-up your answer to the talk question, and say why.
talk.action: Pause. Explain your answer to someone at home, with a reason.

exit.say: Recording: pause and do the exit ticket on your own. Then press play to check it.
exit.action: Pause. Do the exit ticket alone, then play to check it.

look.say: Recording: pause and fill in your look-back box. You can pass.
look.action: Pause. Fill in the look-back box, or pass.

flex.say: Recording: well done for finishing! Show a grown-up one thing you found out.
flex.action: Show a grown-up your workbook and tell them one thing you found out.

lines.text: Greet the whole group warmly, before the recording starts. Check that you can see each child, or ask the grown-up.
Hello, inquirers! Pencil ready, and your kit of bars and squares on the table. Cameras can be on or off, as you like.
This lesson is recorded so a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted. You may keep your microphone and camera off.
Start the recording now. Do not use children's first names on the recording.
@rec
Microphone off until I ask you to speak. To answer, say it with me on three, show fingers, or give a thumbs up. Nobody holds paper up to the camera.
Picture a frog on a path of numbers. It can take a big jump of ten, or a small hop of one. Today we plan the frog's journey, and we find out which digit it changes.
Greet the whole group warmly. Do not use children's first names on the recording.

Keep this to two minutes. Say the recording statement and the microphone routine in the same words every lesson, for anyone who joined late. The frog is only a story to hook the idea: the jumps and hops are done with the kit.
@rec
Stand up if you can. We clap on every number. Count in tens with me: ten, twenty, thirty, all the way to one hundred.
Tutor counts in tens and claps on every number; children count quietly along with microphones off and clap on screen.
Now a new start. We begin at three and add ten each time: three, thirteen, twenty-three. Point to the tiles as we say them.
Tutor counts on from 3 in tens (3, 13, 23 ... 93) and points at each tile; children say it quietly along.
Look at the numbers. What stays the same every time? Tell your screen.
Tens and ones. A bar is a ten. A square is a one. Four bars and six squares is forty-six.
Fifty-two. How many tens? How many ones?
Seventy. How many tens? How many ones?
Eighty-three. How many tens? How many ones?
Ten and some more. Forty and five more is forty-five. We say the tens, then count on the ones.
Thirty and four more?
Fifty and seven more?
Eighty and two more?

If a child hesitates, say the tens word slowly (thirty... four) and point to the bars and then the squares in the picture. Do not move on until most children have answered: counting on from a tens number is what the lesson uses.

Answers: the ones digit stays 3; then 5 tens 2 ones, 7 tens 0 ones, 8 tens 3 ones; then 34, 57, 82. Children answer with fingers, thumbs or a whispered number. Nobody writes. A child new to bars and squares sees them in the picture first, then says the number.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Mei has the sticks in the picture. Then she gets another bundle of 10 sticks. How many sticks does Mei have now? You may draw.
Children count and write the number on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Ravi says forty-three plus twenty is forty-five. Is Ravi right? Write Yes or No. Then write how you know.
Children write or draw their answer.
Thank you. Keep your paper and your own answer: nobody shows it. We will come back to puzzle two in a few minutes, and you can check your own thinking then.

Puzzle 1 answer: 36 sticks (26 and one more bundle). Puzzle 2 answer: no, 43 + 20 = 63; Ravi added 2 to the ones digit. Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who drew bundles, or who said 20 is 2 tens). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today the kit is a number path in your hands. A bar is a big jump of ten. A square is a small hop of one. Build thirty-four: three bars and four squares.
Children build 34 with bars and squares and show a thumbs up when ready. Tutor waits for most thumbs.
Take a big jump forward: add one bar.
What number do you have now?
Jump again.
And now?
Now jump back: take one bar away.
What number now?
Jump back two more times.
And now?
Which digit changed each time? Which digit stayed the same?
Now the small hops. Start with twenty-four: two bars and four squares. A hop is one square. Hop forward three times: add three squares.
Children build 24 (or take their kit back to 24) and show a thumbs up when ready.
What number now?
Hop back two: take two squares away.
And now?
Which digit changed this time, the tens or the ones?
A jump changes the tens digit. A hop changes the ones digit.
Now jump and hop together. Build thirty-four again. We add twenty-five. Jump twice, then hop five times. Show a thumbs up when you have built it.
Children add 2 bars then 5 squares and show a thumbs up. Answer 59.
Next: forty-one plus thirty-eight. Jump three times, hop eight times.
Build 41, add 3 bars and 8 squares. Answer 79.
Now take away. Build sixty-eight. Take away twenty-four: jump back twice, hop back four times.
Build 68, take away 2 bars and 4 squares. Answer 44.
Now we put the same journey on paper. This is a number line. Draw a dot and write thirty-four. Draw a big arc for the jump of twenty, and write plus twenty. Write where you land.
Children draw the dot, the arc and the landing number 54 on paper. Tutor draws the same line step by step on a shared whiteboard or a blank slide.
Now a small arc for the hop of five. Write plus five, and write where you land.
Children finish the line: 34, +20, 54, +5, 59. Wait for thumbs up. Then redo it for 68 take away 24 with back arcs: 68, -20, 48, -4, 44.
Look at your line. Which arc is big and which is small? Why?
What did you notice? Which one changes the tens, a jump or a hop? Does it matter if you hop first or jump first?
A jump of ten changes the tens digit. A hop of one changes the ones digit. Today we always stay inside a ten: we never go past nine ones.
A child who adds the 2 of 25 to the ones: ask how many squares one bar is worth, then rebuild with 2 bars (the two jumps) and 5 squares (the five hops).
A child with too few bars: they may use 9 bars and 20 squares from the kit page; no more than that is needed in this lesson.

Main room only: no breakout rooms. Keep the picture of jump and hop as ten and one. Never say that you carry or rename; if a child asks what happens when the ones pass nine, say: good question, we will learn that very soon.
@rec

Here is the number path. We start on thirty-four and take a big jump of ten: we land on forty-four. Another jump lands on fifty-four. Two jumps of ten is twenty, so thirty-four plus twenty is fifty-four.
Which digit changed? Which digit stayed the same?
Jumping back takes tens away. From fifty-four, jump back ten: forty-four. Jump back again: thirty-four. Fifty-four take away twenty is thirty-four.
Now you try. Seventy-eight take away thirty. Which way is the jump?
Now the small hops. A hop is one. Thirty-four plus three: hop three times to thirty-seven. The tens digit does not change. Thirty-seven take away two: hop back two to thirty-five.
Is five a jump or a hop?
Jump, then hop. Thirty-four plus twenty-five. Twenty-five is two tens and five ones. First jump two tens: thirty-four to fifty-four. Then hop five: fifty-nine.
How many tens are in thirty-six? How many ones?
Take away works the same way. Fifty-nine take away twenty-five. Jump back two tens: thirty-nine. Hop back five: thirty-four.
What is eighty-seven take away thirty-two? Say the jump first, then the hop.
Your turn. Write the answers on your paper. Forty-five plus thirty. Seventy-eight take away twenty. Sixty-four take away three. Fifty-two plus thirty-six.
Children write four answers. Wait until most have stopped writing.
Seventy-five. Fifty-eight. Sixty-one. Eighty-eight.
Quick-fire. Is it a jump or a hop? Thirty.
Six?
Fifty?
Two?

Key words to use every time: jump (ten), hop (one), tens digit, ones digit. Do not teach carrying or renaming. Every example stays inside a ten: 34 + 25 uses 4 + 5 = 9 ones. Draw the number line on a shared whiteboard or a blank slide as you talk (not on paper under the webcam), so the recording shows the arcs.
If a child writes 35 for 45 + 30 or similar: ask how many bars 30 is, and whether a hop or a jump is needed. Build it with the kit and say the tens first.
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. Find a little space. We start on thirty-four. A big jump for every ten, a small hop for every one. Say the number each time.

Call the moves one at a time and wait for everyone: jump twice (44, 54), hop three times (55, 56, 57), jump back once (47), hop back four times (46, 45, 44, 43). Say each number clearly; children count quietly along.
@rec

Page 1, Start here. Question 1: Mei gets one more bundle of ten. Fill in the bundles, the singles and the number. Question 2: draw 3 tall bars of ten and 4 single sticks, then 2 more tall bars. Question 3: jump forward. Twenty-three plus ten. Twenty-three plus forty. Fifty-one plus thirty. Seven plus sixty.

Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor looks around the gallery, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. Move to the answer slide only when most children have stopped writing; anyone not finished keeps going and checks later.
Answers for page 1. If you are still working, carry on and check later. Thirty-six. Fifty-four. Thirty-three, sixty-three, eighty-one, sixty-seven. Check your own page in another colour.
After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.

Page 2. Question 4: jump or hop. Thirty-four take away ten. Fifty-eight take away twenty. Fifty-eight take away three. Sixty-two plus seven. Question 5: Ali has 68 pencils and gives away 3 boxes of ten. Question 6: Ben says forty-five plus twenty is forty-seven. Is Ben correct? Circle Yes or No. Then fill in the blanks. Question 7: start at 36 and draw two jumps of ten.
Page 2, questions 4 to 7. Move to the answer slide only when most children have stopped writing.

Answers for page 2. If you are still working, carry on and check later. Question 4: twenty-four, thirty-eight, fifty-five, sixty-nine. Question 5: thirty-eight. Question 6: no, sixty-five. Question 7: fifty-six.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time.
Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page.

Q2 (drawing): draw each ten as one tall bar, like the bars in the kit. Q3 and Q4: ask is it a jump or a hop, then say the tens first. Q6: build 45 with the kit and add 2 bars. Q7: draw a dot for 36, then an arc and write +10.

A child who is still stuck ticks I am still stuck on their own look-back page. The grown-up may photograph that page and send it to the business WhatsApp after class. Open the next lesson with one short catch-up question for the whole group. Never a private message to a child, never a private room.

Think harder is for ideas taught today in a new setting (jump and hop together). Go further is for mastery and extension. Do not announce who is on which page. Pairs are never split unless both children agree.
@rec
Mei says: when you jump forward 2 tens, the ones digit changes. Is Mei right? Use your kit to show why.
Build 34 and jump forward 2 tens with the kit. Which digit changed?
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember puzzle two? Ravi said forty-three plus twenty is forty-five. Twenty is two tens, so we jump, we do not hop. Forty-three plus twenty is sixty-three.
Did anyone change their mind about puzzle two while we worked? You can just nod.

Model answer: no. 34 + 20 = 54: the 4 ones are still there. Two tens are two bars, so only the tens digit changes (3 to 5). Volunteers first; never call a child by name to answer; no tallies, no rankings. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Exit ticket. Three questions, on your own, without looking back. Write your answers on page 5. I will read them to you twice.

Question 1: forty-six plus thirty. Question 2: part a, seventy-four take away thirty. Part b, seventy-four take away three. Question 3: Mei is on fifty-two. She jumps forward 2 tens, then hops forward 3. After the jump she is on what? After the hop she is on what?
Children answer E1 to E3 on their own. Remind them they may draw the jumps.
Seventy-six. Forty-four and seventy-one. Fifty-nine.
Tick the ones you got right, in a different colour. Well done. Show your ticket to a grown-up.
Show me with your fingers how many you got right: three, two, one, or none yet. A pass is fine.

Look at the room as a whole, not at any one tile. If many children show one or two fingers, spend two minutes at the start of Lesson 7 on jump and hop, in the open session, no names. Do not write a child's name next to an answer and do not read out anyone's result.
@rec

Look-back. Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. If you like, tick one thing to try next time. If you still need help, tick I am still stuck and show your grown-up. You can pass. Nobody reads it out.
Children fill in the look-back box on page 5.
@rec
Well done, inquirers. Next lesson is Take Away, Count Up. You need your kit, a pencil, a pencil of another colour, paper and an envelope. Goodbye, and thank you to the grown-ups.
Optional, only if you are on time: start at 5 and jump in tens. What is the last number you can reach before one hundred? How many jumps is that?
Short think time, then take two answers.
Spare-time menu. If the whole class is ahead, pick one or two activities from the guide (about 4 minutes each).

This is the standing buffer. If you are behind, finish the look-back and say goodbye. Do not start anything new. Optional slide answer: 95, after 9 jumps (5, 15, 25 ... 95); one more jump would pass one hundred. If the whole class is ahead, use the Spare-time menu (guide section 3b) instead of rushing on.

slides.title: Tens Jump, Ones Hop

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Jump in tens, hop in ones, and say which digit changes.

slides.note: Lesson 6 of Term 1, 90 minutes. Objective: add and take away tens and ones in your head, jumping the tens first and then hopping the ones. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 28, mini-lesson 28 to 38, brain break 38 to 42, workbook 42 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Nobody is told which page they should be on. Tell the group the lesson is recorded (the tutor, the screen and any voice that is not muted) and that a child may keep the microphone and camera off.
slides.subtitle: Adding and taking away tens and ones

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: count in tens

blocks.text: Clap on every number
Now start at 3 and add ten each time.

slides.note: Count in tens to 100 with a clap on each number. Then start at 3 and count on in tens. Ask what stays the same (the ones digit, 3). This is a spiral review of skip counting in tens (holiday topic) and lets a new child join: they hear it before they say it.

slides.title: Tens and ones

blocks.text: A bar is a ten. A square is a one. How many tens? How many ones?

slides.note: Say each number; children say how many tens and how many ones, with fingers or a whispered answer. Answers: 52 is 5 tens and 2 ones, 70 is 7 tens and 0 ones, 83 is 8 tens and 3 ones. Point to the bars and then the squares in the picture. No writing, no marks.

slides.title: Ten and some more

blocks.text: 40 and 5 more is 45. Count on from the tens.

slides.note: Answers: 34, 57, 82. Say the tens word slowly, then count on the ones: forty... forty-one, forty-two. This is the bridge to jumping and hopping. Show the bars as a number path if a child is unsure.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Mei has these sticks.
Then she gets another bundle of 10 sticks.
How many sticks does Mei have now?

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Ravi says 43 + 20 = 45.
Is Ravi right? Write Yes or No. Then write how you know.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (26 sticks and one more bundle) is an access question: any child can try it by counting or drawing. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson's key idea: 20 is 2 tens. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper up to the camera: children keep their own answer and check it at Talk time. No private chat and no board in front of the group. Answers: 36; no, 63. Do not reveal Puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list of who found it easy.

slides.title: Explore: jump with bars

items: Build 34: 3 bars and 4 squares.
A big jump is a bar. Add one bar. Say the number.
Jump again. Say the number.
Jump back: take a bar away. Say the number.

slides.note: Round 1, about 4 minutes. Objects first, no writing. A bar is a big jump of ten. Children build 34, jump forward twice (44, 54), then back (44, 34, then 24). Ask for a thumbs up when the build is ready. Ask which digit changed and which stayed the same. A child with too few bars can use the full kit page: 9 bars and 20 squares are enough for this lesson.

slides.title: Explore: hop with squares

items: Build 24: 2 bars and 4 squares.
A small hop is a square. Hop forward 3 times.
Hop back 2.
Which digit changed?

slides.note: Round 2, about 3 minutes. Hop three squares forward: 27. Hop two back: 25. The ones digit changes and the tens digit stays. Say it in the children's words: a jump changes the tens, a hop changes the ones.

slides.title: Explore: jump and hop

blocks.text: Build the first number. Jump the tens. Then hop the ones. Show a thumbs up when you have built it.

slides.note: Round 3, about 5 minutes. 34 + 25: 2 bars then 5 squares gives 59. 41 + 38: 3 bars then 8 squares gives 79. 68 - 24: take away 2 bars then 4 squares gives 44. Wait for the thumbs up on each build. Say each answer aloud for the recording. A child who adds the 2 as ones is mixing up jump and hop: ask how many squares one bar is worth.

slides.title: Draw the jumps and hops

items: Draw a dot. Write the start number.
Draw a big arc for the jump. Write +20.
Write where you land.
Draw a small arc for the hop. Write +5. Write where you land.

slides.note: Round 4, about 4 minutes. Draw on a shared whiteboard or blank slide as the children draw on paper: dot, arc, landing number. A big arc is a jump of tens, a small arc is a hop of ones. Draw 34 to 59 first, then 68 back to 44 with arcs going back. The paper line is the picture children use in question 7 and in Think harder.  The landing numbers are hidden on this slide: children find them. They appear on the next slide.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: Which one changes the tens digit, a jump or a hop?
Which one changes the ones digit?
Does it matter if you hop first or jump first?
How many ones can we hop before we reach ten?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key ideas: a jump of ten changes the tens digit; a hop of one changes the ones digit; jumping first or hopping first lands in the same place (do not push the proof, the Think harder page tests it); we stay inside a ten today. Repeat a child's answer in your own words so the recording picks it up.

slides.title: Jump forward: add tens

blocks.text: Each jump adds 1 ten. The ones digit stays the same.

slides.note: Point along the number line on the slide as you talk (or redraw it on a shared whiteboard). The arcs are the jumps. Two jumps of ten add 20. Ask: which digit changed? Answer: the tens digit, 3 to 5. The 4 ones stay.

slides.title: Jump back: take away tens

blocks.text: Each jump back takes away 1 ten. The ones digit stays the same.

slides.note: The same picture backwards. Arcs go back, so the numbers get smaller. Say: 54 take away 10 is 44, take away 10 again is 34. Link to the kit: take two bars away.

slides.title: Hop: ones

blocks.text: A hop changes the ones digit. The tens digit stays.

slides.note: Small hops of one. Show a hop as a small arc and a jump as a big arc. Ask: is five a jump or a hop? Answer: a hop, it is ones. Keep every example inside a ten: no hop may pass nine ones today.

slides.title: Jump, then hop: add

blocks.text: 25 is 2 tens and 5 ones. Jump the tens first. Then hop the ones.

slides.note: Worked example. Split 25 into 20 and 5. Jump 20 from 34 to 54, then hop 5 to 59. Ask: how many tens and how many ones in 36? (3 tens, 6 ones) to check children can split a number. The example stays inside a ten (4 + 5 = 9). Do not mention carrying or renaming.

slides.title: Jump, then hop: take away

blocks.text: 25 is 2 tens and 5 ones. Jump back the tens first. Then hop back the ones.

slides.note: Worked example. 59 - 25: jump back 20 to 39, then hop back 5 to 34. The arcs go backwards, so the numbers get smaller. Ask: what is 87 - 32? Answer: jump back 3 tens to 57, hop back 2 to 55. Stay inside a ten (9 - 5 = 4, 7 - 2 = 5).

slides.title: Your turn: write the answer

blocks.text: Write on your paper. About 2 minutes

slides.note: Each child writes on their own paper. Wait until most children have stopped writing. Do not ask children to hold boards up in front of the group. Children may draw the jump or use the kit. Answers are on the next slide.

slides.title: Check: write the answer
slides.note: Answers: 75, 58, 61, 88. Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Ask which were jumps, which were hops and which needed both (the third is a hop, the fourth is a jump then a hop).

slides.title: Jump or hop?

blocks.text: Tens are a jump. Ones are a hop.

slides.note: Quick-fire. Say a number and ask: jump or hop? Answers: 30 jump, 6 hop, 50 jump, 2 hop. A multiple of ten is a jump because it is whole bars. Keep it quick: this is the decision children make on the workbook pages.

slides.title: Jump the tens, hop the ones

blocks.text: A big jump for every ten. A small hop for every one.

blocks.head: START ON 34
items: Jump forward 2 times.
Hop forward 3 times.
Jump back 1 time.
Hop back 4 times.

blocks.text: Say the number each time. Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera with a little clear space; no stairs and no running. Start on 34: jump forward twice (44, 54), hop forward three times (55, 56, 57), jump back once (47), hop back four times (46, 45, 44, 43). Count the numbers aloud together. Keep it gentle for small spaces. No equipment.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. About 9 minutes

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: MEI SAYS
items: When you jump forward 2 tens, the ones digit changes.

blocks.text: Is Mei right? Use your kit to show why.
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: no. 34 + 20 = 54, and the 4 ones are still there. Two tens are two bars, so only the tens digit changes. Repeat each child's answer in your own words for the recording.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: No. 43 + 20 = 63. Twenty is 2 tens, so we jump.

slides.note: Reveal puzzle 2 now. Say: some of you may have found a good reason. Ravi hopped 2 ones (45) instead of jumping 2 tens (63). Do not read out anyone's earlier answer.

How many jumps is that?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. Answer: 95, after 9 jumps (5, 15, 25 ... 95). One more jump would pass one hundred, which we meet in the next lessons. Take two answers and move on.

blocks.text: Optional. Everyone may join.

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. start.text: These are Mei’s sticks. She gets another bundle of 10 sticks. Fill in the blanks.

parts.text: Now Mei has ___ bundles of ten.

start.hint: Count the bundles in tens: 10, 20, 30. Then count on the 7 singles.
start.solution: The picture shows 2 bundles and 7 singles, which is 27. One more bundle makes 3 bundles, and the 7 singles stay. 30 and 7 is 37.
mistakes: Adding the bundle to the singles (28).

start.text: In the box, draw 3 tens as 3 tall bars and 4 single sticks. Next, draw 2 more tall bars. How many sticks are there altogether?
start.hint: A bundle of ten is a tall bar, like the bars in your kit. Draw 3 bars, then 4 short lines, then 2 more bars.
start.solution: 3 bars and 4 singles is 34. Two more bars add 20, so there are 5 bars and 4 singles: 54.
mistakes: Drawing 2 sticks instead of 2 bars of ten.

start.text: Jump forward. Fill in the blanks.
start.hint: Think of the tens as bars. 23 + 10 is one more bar. The ones digit stays the same.
start.solution: (a) 2 tens and 1 ten make 3 tens: 33. (b) 2 tens and 4 tens make 6 tens: 63. (c) 5 tens and 3 tens make 8 tens: 81. (d) 7 is 7 ones; add 6 tens to get 67.

start.text: Jump or hop. Fill in the blanks.
start.hint: A tens number is a jump. A ones number is a hop. Say which one it is before you work it out.
start.solution: (a) 3 tens take away 1 ten is 2 tens: 24. (b) 5 tens take away 2 tens is 3 tens: 38. (c) 3 is a hop: 8 ones take away 3 is 5 ones: 55. (d) 7 is a hop forward: 2 and 7 make 9 ones: 69.
mistakes: Taking the 3 from the tens digit (58 - 3 = 28).

start.text: Ali has 68 pencils. He gives 3 boxes of 10 pencils to his friend. How many pencils does Ali have left?
start.hint: 3 boxes of ten is 30 pencils. Jump back 3 tens from 68.
start.solution: 3 boxes of ten is 30 pencils. 68 - 30 = 38: jump back 3 tens (58, 48, 38). The 8 ones stay.

start.text: Ben says 45 + 20 = 47. Fill in a to c.

parts.text: Is Ben correct? Circle Yes or No.
Ben added 2 ___ by mistake. He should add 2 ___.

start.answer: No. The right answer is 65. He added 2 ones instead of 2 tens.
start.hint: Build 45 with the kit. Is 20 two bars or two squares?
start.solution: 20 is 2 tens, so Ben should jump two tens: 45, 55, 65. He added 2 ones and got 47. A jump changes the tens digit.
mistakes: Saying he is correct because 20 has a 2 in it.
Not saying what he mixed up (any clear sentence about tens and ones is fine).

start.text: Show 2 jumps of ten on the number line, beginning at 36. Where do you land?
start.hint: Draw a dot for 36. Draw an arc to the right and write +10. Do it once more.
start.solution: 36 + 10 = 46, then 46 + 10 = 56. Two jumps of ten land on 56. The 6 ones never change.

think.hint: First jump 4 tens from 23. Where are you? Then hop 5 ones.
think.solution: 45 is 4 tens and 5 ones. 23 + 40 = 63. Then 63 + 5 = 68. Check: 2 tens and 4 tens are 6 tens; 3 ones and 5 ones are 8 ones.
mistakes: Adding only the tens and stopping at 63.

think.answer: 44 (jump back 30 to 49, then hop back 5 to 44)
think.hint: Jump back 3 tens from 79. Then hop back 5.
mistakes: Taking 35 away from the ones only.

think.text: Both frogs start on 12. Frog A jumps 3 tens, then hops 4. Frog B hops 4, then jumps 3 tens. Fill in a to c.

parts.text: Is the landing number the same for both frogs? Circle Yes or No.

think.answer: Yes, both land on 46 (30 and 4 are added in either order)
think.hint: Find where Frog A lands. Then Frog B. Compare.
think.solution: Frog A: 12 + 30 = 42, then 42 + 4 = 46. Frog B: 12 + 4 = 16, then 16 + 30 = 46. They land on the same number: adding the same jumps and hops in a different order gives the same total.
mistakes: Saying Frog B lands on 16 because the hops came first.

think.text: Ali starts on a number. He jumps forward 3 tens and ends on 78. Where did Ali start?
think.hint: Go backwards. Undo the jumps: jump back 3 tens from 78.
think.solution: Undo the 3 jumps of ten: 78, 68, 58, 48. Check: 48 + 30 = 78.

go.text: Mei is on 7 and must get to 97. Each time she can jump 10 or jump 20. Many answers are right. Fill in a and b.

parts.text: Write the numbers Mei lands on in one way.
parts.ans: any way that adds up to 90

parts.text: Write the numbers for a different way.

go.answer: Any two different routes of 10s and 20s from 7 to 97, e.g. 7, 17, 27, 37, 47, 57, 67, 77, 87, 97 (nine jumps of 10) and 7, 27, 47, 67, 87, 97 (four of 20 and one of 10).
go.hint: The jumps must add up to 90. Check each landing number: it is 10 or 20 more than the one before.
go.solution: Every jump adds 10 or 20, and all the jumps together add 90 (97 - 7). Examples: nine jumps of 10; or 20, 20, 20, 20, 10 landing on 27, 47, 67, 87, 97. The ones digit stays 7 on every landing.
mistakes: Landing on a number that is not 10 or 20 more than the one before.
Two routes that are the same jumps in the same order.

go.text: Now Mei wants the fewest jumps from 7 to 97. She can jump 10 or jump 20. Use the line in G1. Fill in a and b.

parts.text: The fewest number of jumps is ___.
Why can Mei not do it in 4 jumps? I know because ___.
parts.ans: Four jumps of 20 make only 80, so she would reach 87.

go.answer: 5 jumps: four jumps of 20 and one jump of 10 (any order). Four jumps travel at most 80, so she reaches only 87.
go.hint: 90 is 9 tens. A jump of 20 is 2 tens. How many jumps of 20 fit?
go.solution: She must travel 9 tens. Four jumps of 20 make 8 tens. One jump of 10 makes the last ten. That is 5 jumps. Four jumps can travel at most 80, which only reaches 87, so 5 is the fewest.

go.text: Start at 25. Jump forward 3 tens, jump back 1 ten, then jump forward 2 tens. Then hop and land on 69. Fill in a to c.

parts.text: Write each number you land on before the hop.
The three jumps are the same as one jump of ___ tens forward.

go.answer: 55, 45, 65, then a hop of 4 to 69. The three jumps are the same as 4 tens forward.
go.hint: Do one move at a time and write where you land each time. Then look at 65 and 69.
go.solution: 25 + 30 = 55. 55 - 10 = 45. 45 + 20 = 65. To land on 69 the hop is 4. Short way: 3 - 1 + 2 = 4 tens forward, so 25 + 40 = 65.
mistakes: Jumping forward on the jump back.

investigation.title: Jump road
investigation.first: Start at 6. Jump in tens 5 times. Write every number you land on.
investigation.text: Start at 6 and keep jumping in tens. Will you land on 50? Write Yes or No. Then try other start numbers from 0 to 50. Which start numbers can land on 50? Write what you notice.
investigation.answer: From 6 you land on 16, 26, 36, 46, 56 and so on: every number ends in 6, so you never land on 50. Jumps of ten never change the ones digit. Only a start number that ends in 0 (0, 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 itself) can land on 50.
investigation.look_for: A child who tests more than one start number, says the ones digit stays the same, and gives a reason using tens and ones (a jump is whole bars). A child who says start 20 can land on 50 because 20 + 30 = 50.
mistakes: Saying you can land on any number.

talk.question: Mei says: when you jump forward 2 tens, the ones digit changes. Is Mei right? Use your kit to show why.
talk.answer: No. 34 + 20 = 54, and the 4 ones are still there. Two tens are 2 bars, so only the tens digit changes, from 3 to 5.
talk.look_for: A reason that uses bars or tens (not just "because I added").

exit.solution: 4 tens and 3 tens make 7 tens. The 6 ones stay: 76.
(a) 30 is 3 tens: jump back to 44. (b) 3 is a hop: hop back to 71.
mistakes: Doing the same for both parts.

exit.text: Mei is on 52. She jumps forward 2 tens, then hops forward 3. Fill in the blanks.

parts.text: After the jump she is on ___.
After the hop she is on ___.

exit.solution: 2 tens forward from 52 is 72. Then a hop of 3 forward is 75.

hardest: knowing if it is a jump or a hop

home_practice.text: A box has 4 bundles of 10 pencils and 5 single pencils. Ali puts in 3 more bundles of 10. How many pencils are in the box now?
home_practice.solution: 4 tens and 3 tens make 7 tens. The 5 loose pencils stay: 75.
40 is 4 tens, a jump back: 46. 4 is a hop back: 82.

home_practice.text: Ravi and Mei each have 53 stickers. Ravi gives away 3. Mei gives away 30. (a) Ravi has ___ stickers left. (b) Mei has ___ stickers left.
home_practice.solution: Ravi hops back 3: 50. Mei jumps back 3 tens: 23.

home_practice.text: Add 36 + 23 in two ways: (a) jump first, then hop; (b) hop first, then jump. Is the answer the same? Circle Yes or No.
home_practice.solution: Jump first: 36 + 20 = 56, then + 3 = 59. Hop first: 36 + 3 = 39, then + 20 = 59.

home_practice.text: (a) On spare paper, draw a number line from 0 to 100. Put a coin on 7 and jump it in tens. Write each number. (b) What stays the same?
home_practice.answer: 7, 17, 27 ... 97. The ones digit stays the same.
home_practice.solution: A grown-up checks that each number is 10 more than the one before. The ones digit never changes when you jump in tens.

slips.say: 36 is 34 + 2. 20 is 2 tens, not 2 ones. Jump, do not hop.
74 is 34 + 40. Two tens is 20, so jump 2 times.

tpl.hint: {k} is {m} tens. Jump forward {m} tens. The ones digit stays {o}.

slips.say: 56 is 58 - 2. 20 is 2 tens, so jump back 2 tens.
78 is 58 + 20. Take away, jump back.

tpl.hint: {k} is {m} tens. Jump back {m} tens. The ones digit stays {o}.

items.hint: 3 is a hop. Hop forward 3 ones.

slips.say: 64 is 34 + 30. A hop of 3 adds 3 ones, not 3 tens.

tpl.hint: {p} is a hop. Hop forward {p} ones. The tens digit stays {t}.

items.hint: 3 is a hop. Hop back 3 ones.

slips.say: 17 is 47 - 30. A hop of 3 takes away 3 ones, not 3 tens.

tpl.hint: {p} is a hop. Hop back {p} ones. The tens digit stays {t}.

items.q: Which one is a jump of ten, not a hop?
items.hint: A jump is a number of tens, like 10, 20 or 30.
steps: 30 is 3 tens, so it is a jump.
3, 8 and 2 are ones, so they are hops.

slips.say: 3 is 3 ones: a hop. Look for a tens number.

items.q: Mei has 34 stickers. She gets 2 packs of 10 stickers. How many stickers does Mei have now?
items.hint: 2 packs of ten is 20 stickers. Jump forward 2 tens.

slips.say: 36 is 34 + 2. A pack of ten is worth 10, so jump.

tpl.q: Mei has {n} stickers. She gets {m} packs of 10 stickers. How many stickers does Mei have now?
tpl.hint: {m} packs of ten is {k} stickers. Jump forward {m} tens.

slips.say: 54 is only the jump. Do not forget the hop of 5.
74 is 7 tens and 4 ones: you added 2 + 5 as tens. 25 is 2 tens and 5 ones.

items.hint: Split 24 into 20 and 4. Jump back 20 first.

slips.say: 48 is only the jump back. Do not forget the hop of 4.
92 is 68 + 24. Take away.

tpl.hint: Split {a} into {k} and {p}. Jump back {k} first.

items.q: Frog A starts on 12. It jumps 3 tens, then hops 4. Frog B starts on 12. It hops 4, then jumps 3 tens. Which sentence is true?
options: They land on the same number
items.answer: They land on the same number
steps: Both land on 46: the order does not matter.

slips.say: Check both frogs. B hops first (16), then jumps 30 to 46, just like A.

items.q: Ali jumps forward 3 tens and ends on 78. Where did he start?
items.hint: Go backwards: jump back 3 tens from 78.

slips.say: 108 is 78 + 30. Undo means go back.
75 is 78 - 3. 3 tens is 30.

tpl.q: Ali jumps forward {m} tens and ends on {n}. Where did he start?
tpl.hint: Go backwards: jump back {m} tens from {n}.

items.q: Mei is on 7. She jumps in tens until she gets to 97. How many jumps does she make?
items.hint: Jump from 7 in tens: 17, 27, ... and count.
steps: Count the jumps, not the numbers.

slips.say: 10 counts the start number too. Count the jumps between the numbers.
90 is how far she travels, not how many jumps.

tpl.q: Mei is on {a}. She jumps in tens until she gets to {b}. How many jumps does she make?
tpl.hint: Jump from {a} in tens and count the jumps.

items.q: Mei goes from 7 to 97 using only jumps of 10 and jumps of 20. What is the fewest number of jumps she can make?
items.hint: 90 is 9 tens. A jump of 20 is 2 tens. How many fit?
steps: Four jumps of 20 make 8 tens, plus one jump of 10.

slips.say: Four jumps of 20 only reach 87. She needs one more.
9 uses only jumps of 10. Use the bigger jumps.

tpl.q: Mei goes from {a} to {b} using only jumps of 10 and jumps of 20. What is the fewest number of jumps she can make?
tpl.hint: {t} tens to travel. A jump of 20 is 2 tens.
steps: Use as many jumps of 20 as she can, and a jump of 10 if one ten is left.

items.q: Start at 25. Jump forward 3 tens, jump back 1 ten, then hop forward 4. Where do you land?
items.hint: Do one move at a time and write where you land.

slips.say: 45 is before the hop of 4. Do the last move too.
29 is 25 + 4. Do the jumps as well.

tpl.q: Start at {s}. Jump forward {a} tens, jump back {b} tens, then hop forward {c}. Where do you land?
tpl.hint: Do one move at a time and write where you land.

items.q: Make up your own jump and hop puzzle with a start number, a jump and a hop. Find where you land, then ask a grown-up to check.
items.hint: Pick a start number first. Choose a jump of tens and a hop of ones that does not pass a ten.
steps: Write the start number, the jump and the hop.
Find where you land with your kit or a number line.
Swap with a grown-up. Do you land on the same number? Example: start at 23, jump 3 tens, hop 4 ones: 23 + 30 = 53, then 57.

parent.summary: We added and took away tens and ones in our heads. A jump of ten changes only the tens digit. A hop of one changes only the ones digit. For 34 + 25, jump the tens, then hop the ones. Term 1 goes beyond the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose: we start every idea with bars and number lines, and your child chooses how far to go. Each week we suggest Home Practice (about 15 minutes); pages 3 to 5 and online practice are optional.
words: jump: add or take away tens (10, 20, 30 ...)
hop: add or take away ones (1, 2, 3 ...)
tens digit: the left digit, it counts the tens
ones digit: the right digit, it counts the ones
try_home: Jump and hop: pick a number up to 60 whose ones digit is 1 to 6, such as a door or page number. Ask: what is 10 more? 20 more? 3 more? Let your child build it with bars and squares if they want.
Number path: draw a line on paper with a mark every 10. Put a coin on a number and jump it in tens. Ask which digit changes and which stays the same.
Silly mistake: say 34 + 20 = 36 on purpose and let your child find what went wrong.
ask: Is that a jump or a hop?
What do you land on after the jump?
parent.when_stuck: Let your child use the bars and squares or draw the jumps, and wait 10 seconds before helping. Please do not teach the column method yet, and do not hurry. If your child ticked I am still stuck on the look-back page, photograph that page and send it to the business WhatsApp, +65 9880 5962, after class. Photos are kept for 90 days after the program ends, then deleted.
parent.next: Lesson 7: Take Away, Count Up. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted; your child may mute and keep the camera off. The recording link is private to your family: please do not share it.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to add and take away tens and ones in their head and to say why. This week: jumping in tens and hopping in ones.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones, to notice patterns and to say why.
next_materials: Your tens bars and ones squares, cut out (workbook page 6) and kept in an envelope
A pencil, a pencil of another colour, a rubber and spare paper

safeguarding: Small things stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. The kit is paper, so there is nothing to swallow.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.

Nobody holds paper or work up to the camera: a gallery view shows everyone. Children tick their own work against the answer slide, answer together on three, or show fingers or a thumb for a choice. There is no private chat and no board held up in front of the group.
Movement break: children need a little clear space, soft shoes or socks on a safe floor, no stairs and no running. A child may march on the spot or stay seated.

Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. The recording captures the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted. Children may mute and keep their cameras off. Never show a child's page on the recording.

A child who needs help ticks I am still stuck on their own look-back page. The grown-up may photograph that page and send it to the program's business WhatsApp after class (never to a personal phone); the tutor replies to the grown-up only. The next lesson starts with one short catch-up question for the whole group. No private messages to children and no private room.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first. Draw number lines on a shared whiteboard or a blank slide, not on paper under the webcam, which the recording cannot show.
Tell parents a week before: print workbook pages 1 to 6, find the kit bars and squares from Lesson 1 (or cut out page 6 again), and a pencil and spare paper.
Have the slides open. The slides show number lines with jump arcs; draw the arcs on the shared whiteboard as well.

Test the recording once with several tiles before the first live class: check that it captures the tutor, the shared screen and any unmuted voice, and not the children's faces. Write the setting you used in your tutor notes.

Say plainly if a parent asks: Term 1 goes beyond the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose. Every Start here item is built to be reached with bars, bundles or a number line and a worked step, and the program does not claim to match any school syllabus. Items that need more than that sit at Think harder.

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content. If you are more than 3 minutes ahead at minute 42, use one menu activity then.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask How do you know? and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: when you add a ten, only the tens digit changes. Try 34, 67 and 90 with your kit. What do you notice?
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Try adding ten to 34, 67 and 90. What do you notice?
menu.answer: For 34 and 67 only the tens digit changes: 44 and 77. For 90 + 10 the answer is 100: ten tens, a number we meet properly later.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Pick a start number. Write one jump and one hop, like start at 23, jump 3 tens, hop 4. Give it to your grown-up to solve.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Write a jump and hop puzzle for a grown-up to solve.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check that the puzzle has a start number, a jump of tens and a hop of ones that stays inside a ten. Example: 23 + 30 + 4 = 57.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never seen jumps and hops. Teach them how to find 52 + 31.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how to find 52 + 31 with a jump and a hop.
menu.answer: 31 is 3 tens and 1 one. Jump 3 tens: 52 to 82. Hop 1: 83.
